images.title: 6 rows of 14 split into 10 columns and 4 columns
images.purpose: Show that splitting 14 into 10 and 4 splits the array into two blocks whose packets, 60 and 24, add up to the whole 84.
images.composition: One array of 6 rows split by a dashed line into a block of 10 columns and a block of 4 columns, with the small products and their sum written below.
images.exact_structure: Plain white frame, 1456 by 816. One array of exactly 84 butter packets in 6 rows of 14 columns, split by a gap into two blocks. Every packet is a square 52 by 52 px (corner radius 6 px) with a thin dark #2B2B2B outline and no marking; neighbouring packets are 4 px apart across and down. LEFT block: the first 10 columns, exactly 60 packets filled teal #0072B2, top left corner at x 324 and y 230, spanning x 324 to 880 and y 230 to 562. RIGHT block: the last 4 columns, exactly 24 packets filled amber #E69F00, top left corner at x 908 and y 230, spanning x 908 to 1128 and y 230 to 562. Between the blocks, centred at x 894, one dashed grey #6B7280 vertical line (3 px) from y 215 to y 577. Above the blocks, centred over each block at y 190, in dark #1F2937 bold sans-serif (40 px): 10 columns above the left block (centred at x 602) and 4 columns above the right block (centred at x 1018). At the left of the array, right aligned at x 300 and centred at y 396, the label 6 rows (40 px dark bold). Under the blocks at y 625 (40 px dark bold): 6 × 10 = 60 centred at x 602 and 6 × 4 = 24 centred at x 1018. Under both, centred at x 726 and y 715 in 56 px bold dark: 60 + 24 = 84. In all there are 84 packets, none missing. No other text anywhere. Nothing else in the frame.

images.takeaway: Split one number, multiply each part, add the parts: 6 × 14 = 60 + 24 = 84.
images.description: An array of 84 butter packets, 6 rows of 14, split into a block of 10 columns and a block of 4 columns, with 6 × 10 = 60, 6 × 4 = 24 and 60 + 24 = 84 written under it.
images.context: Concept image for Break a Number into Parts. It follows the idea of the figures in your maths book (an array of packets split into two blocks) and uses the numbers of this concept's own example: 6 and 14.
images.teaching_notes: Let the student count the packets of each block and add them. The slip to watch: multiplying only one of the two parts and forgetting the other block.

image_decisions.why: The array split into two blocks shows that the two small products add up to the whole, which words alone do not.
